raw_text:
### Cardiac Amyloidosis: Evolving Paradigms in Diagnosis and Therapy

#### Introduction and Classification
Systemic amyloidosis comprises a heterogeneous group of disorders defined by the extracellular deposition of misfolded, insoluble protein fibrils in various organs, leading to progressive structural and functional disruption [1]. In the heart, this infiltrative process results in a classic restrictive cardiomyopathy, typically characterized by rapidly progressive diastolic dysfunction, conduction disturbances, and eventually refractory heart failure [2]. Although more than 30 amyloidogenic precursor proteins have been identified, cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is almost exclusively caused by two types: immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) amyloidosis and transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis [3]. AL amyloidosis is a hematologic malignancy arising from clonal plasma cell dyscrasias that produce unstable monoclonal free light chains [4]. Conversely, ATTR amyloidosis is driven by the misfolding of transthyretin, a tetrameric transport protein synthesized primarily by the liver [5]. ATTR can occur either as a wild-type form (ATTRwt), primarily affecting older adults, or as a hereditary variant (ATTRv) caused by autosomal dominant mutations in the *TTR* gene [6].

#### Clinical Suspicion and the "Great Masquerader"
Historically considered a rare and untreatable orphan disease, CA is frequently misdiagnosed as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or hypertensive heart disease [7]. Recent studies have revealed that ATTRwt is a surprisingly common cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) [8] and severe aortic stenosis in older populations [9]. Due to its heterogeneous clinical features, a high index of clinical suspicion is paramount. Clinicians must recognize characteristic "red flags" to initiate diagnostic investigations [10]. These red flags include unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), low QRS voltages on electrocardiography despite marked LVH, carpal tunnel syndrome (often bilateral and preceding cardiac symptoms by years), lumbar spinal stenosis, and autonomic neuropathy [9,10].

#### Diagnostic Advances and Non-Biopsy Criteria
The diagnostic landscape of CA has been revolutionized by advances in cardiovascular imaging and the development of non-invasive diagnostic algorithms. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging is highly sensitive, providing comprehensive tissue characterization [11]. It characteristically demonstrates diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) and marked elevations in native T1 relaxation times and extracellular volume (ECV) fraction [12]. Furthermore, multimodality imaging guidelines [13] have established nuclear scintigraphy using bone-seeking radiotracers—such as Technetium-99m-pyrophosphate ($^{99\text{m}}\text{Tc-PYP}$) [14] or Technetium-99m-3,3-diphosphono-1,2-propanodicarboxylic acid ($^{99\text{m}}\text{Tc-DPD}$) [15]—as a cornerstone of non-invasive evaluation. In patients without a detectable monoclonal protein, a Grade 2 or 3 myocardial tracer uptake on bone scintigraphy combined with single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) has a specificity and positive predictive value of nearly 100% for ATTR-CA, bypassing the absolute historical requirement for endomyocardial biopsy [16]. Crucially, before concluding a diagnosis of ATTR, clonal plasma cell disorders must be systematically excluded using serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis and the serum free light chain (FLC) assay [16].

#### Risk Stratification and Evolving Prognosis
Accurate prognostication is critical for guiding therapeutic interventions. In AL-CA, risk stratification relies heavily on serum biomarkers, including N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) and cardiac troponins [17]. These cardiac markers reflect both the mechanical infiltration of fibrils and the direct cardiotoxicity exerted by circulating free light chains [17]. Therapeutic response in AL-CA is defined by a rapid reduction in the involved FLC clone, which is strongly associated with subsequent organ improvement and prolonged survival [18]. In ATTR-CA, disease-modifying therapies have dramatically reshaped patient outcomes, making early diagnosis a major determinant of long-term prognosis [19,20].

#### Therapeutic Innovations
The therapeutic approach to CA involves targeting the specific precursor protein. In AL-CA, standard chemotherapy regimens have been transformed by the addition of the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody daratumumab, combined with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone (Dara-CyBorD), which induces rapid and deep hematologic remissions [18]. 

In ATTR-CA, the therapeutic arsenal includes transthyretin stabilizers and gene-silencing therapies. Tafamidis, an oral small-molecule TTR stabilizer, was shown in the pivotal ATTR-ACT trial to significantly reduce all-cause mortality and cardiovascular-related hospitalizations in both ATTRwt and ATTRv patients [19]. For patients with ATTRv polyneuropathy, RNA interference (RNAi) agents such as patisiran [20] and antisense oligonucleotides such as inotersen [21] suppress hepatic TTR production. More recently, the APOLLO-B trial demonstrated that patisiran also improves functional capacity and quality of life in patients with ATTR-CA [22]. Additionally, the landmark HELIOS-B trial showed that vutrisiran, a next-generation subcutaneously administered RNAi therapeutic, significantly reduces the composite risk of all-cause mortality and recurrent cardiovascular events in patients with ATTR-CA [23].

#### Conclusion and Future Directions
The shift in CA from a neglected, fatal condition to a treatable disease highlights the importance of patient-centered, multidisciplinary clinics [24]. While conventional heart failure therapies (e.g., beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors) are often poorly tolerated due to restrictive physiology and autonomic dysfunction [25], the emergence of disease-modifying therapies has fundamentally rewritten the natural history of this disease [26,27]. Future efforts must focus on population-level screening in high-risk HFpEF cohorts [28] to ensure early detection. Ongoing clinical trials of novel agents, including gene editing (CRISPR/Cas9) and monoclonal antibodies designed to clear pre-existing amyloid deposits [29], promise to further transform the prognosis of cardiac amyloidosis [30].
